edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe turns from the quoted decree to direct imperative address, opening amid the summons “Now therefore be wise, you kings. Be instructed, you judges of the earth” (web:Ps.2.10), continuing with עִבְד֣וּ (web:Ps.2.11 = oshb:Ps.2.11, byte tier), “Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (web:Ps.2.11), through to the closing warning and blessing, “Give sincere homage to the Son… Blessed are all those who take refuge in him” (web:Ps.2.12). The imperative cluster addressed to “kings” and “judges of the earth” has no antecedent in the decree strophe that precedes it (web:Ps.2.7-web:Ps.2.9), marking a clean seam at web:Ps.2.9-web:Ps.2.10.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching web:Ps.2.10-web:Ps.2.12 to the preceding decree strophe was considered but rejected because the imperative address to earthly kings and judges is a new rhetorical move without antecedent in web:Ps.2.7-web:Ps.2.9.

the closing beatitude at web:Ps.2.12 supplies the second leg of a candidate ashrei frame with web:Ps.1.1, disclosed in device_notes
edited_rows.device_notes: This closing row completes Psalm 2's four-strophe parent grouping. Its word אַ֝שְׁרֵ֗י (web:Ps.2.12 = oshb:Ps.2.12, byte tier) opens the verse's final colon — word 11 of 14, with three words following it, כָּל ח֥וֹסֵי בֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.2.12) — echoing Psalm 1's opening אַ֥שְֽׁרֵי (web:Ps.1.1 = oshb:Ps.1.1, byte tier). The two tokens differ by a meteg (U+05BD present at Ps.1.1's token, absent at Ps.2.12's), which the accent_stripped tier retains by design, so the pair matches at 1 of 4 collation tiers (skeleton), completing a candidate ashrei inclusio around the Psalter's untitled double proem; Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 keep separate parents, and the frame is recorded here as a cross-psalm relation, not a merge.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 4's title (web:Ps.4.0 = oshb:Ps.4.1) marks it lamnatseach, on stringed instruments, le-David, and its eight verses alternate address between Yahweh and the addressee named “sons of men” (web:Ps.4.2) without settling into blocks large enough to divide: the opening plea to Yahweh (web:Ps.4.1) gives way to one unbroken four-verse run addressed to that human audience — the rebuke closed by Selah (web:Ps.4.2, oshb:Ps.4.3), the imperative “know that Yahweh has set apart for himself him who is godly” (web:Ps.4.3, oshb:Ps.4.4), and the further imperative closed by Selah (web:Ps.4.4-web:Ps.4.5, oshb:Ps.4.5-oshb:Ps.4.6) — before direct address to Yahweh resumes at web:Ps.4.6 (oshb:Ps.4.7) and carries through to the close (web:Ps.4.6-web:Ps.4.8). This alternating address argues for treating the psalm as one row rather than dividing it at a particular point. The psalm also opens immediately after the Selah that closes Psalm 3 (web:Ps.3.8 = oshb:Ps.3.9), so that front-seam pause is disclosed here though it belongs to the preceding psalm.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A strophe break between the address to Yahweh and the rebuke of the sons of men was considered but rejected because both addressees recur more than once across the eight verses rather than occupying separate blocks.
observed_substrate_signals: title ref web:Ps.4.0 = oshb:Ps.4.1 with labels mizmor, lamnatseach, le-David

the addressee alternates between Yahweh (web:Ps.4.1, web:Ps.4.6-web:Ps.4.8) and 'sons of men' (web:Ps.4.2, web:Ps.4.4-web:Ps.4.5) without settling into one sustained block for either audience

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 7's title (web:Ps.7.0 = oshb:Ps.7.1) is the psalm's shiggaion, le-David, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite, and the strophe moves from the opening plea for rescue, “I take refuge in you. Save me from all those who pursue me, and deliver me” (web:Ps.7.1), through the lion simile (web:Ps.7.2) into a self-imprecatory oath, “if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands” (web:Ps.7.3), that runs through the conditional curse closed by Selah, “let the enemy pursue my soul, and overtake it… lay my glory in the dust” (web:Ps.7.5, oshb:Ps.7.6). The oath's conditional structure sets this block apart from the imperative summons beginning web:Ps.7.6.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the opening plea (web:Ps.7.1-web:Ps.7.2) from the oath (web:Ps.7.3-web:Ps.7.5) as separate rows was considered but rejected because the oath's protasis in web:Ps.7.3 directly continues the plea's self-referential voice without an address shift.

the oath's conditional clauses run from web:Ps.7.3 to the Selah-closed curse at web:Ps.7.5 (oshb:Ps.7.6), the psalm's one Selah occurrence

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe opens the imperative summons for divine judgment, ק֘וּמָ֤ה (web:Ps.7.6 = oshb:Ps.7.7, byte tier), “Arise, Yahweh, in your anger” (web:Ps.7.6), through the appeal “Judge me, Yahweh, according to my righteousness” (web:Ps.7.8) to the declarative confidence that closes the block, “God is a righteous judge, yes, a God who has indignation every day” (web:Ps.7.11). The strophe ends before the shift to third-person description beginning web:Ps.7.12.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.7.12-web:Ps.7.13 was considered but rejected: the wicked man's unambiguous third-person onset is marked instead by the presentative הִנֵּ֥ה opening web:Ps.7.14 (oshb:Ps.7.15), since third-person declaration about God is already in force one verse before this strophe's own close, at web:Ps.7.11 (oshb:Ps.7.12).

edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe turns to the fate of the wicked, opening אִם לֹ֣א (web:Ps.7.12 = oshb:Ps.7.13, byte tier), “If a man doesn't repent, he will sharpen his sword” (web:Ps.7.12) — the MT's bare third-person verbs carry 0 nominal subjects; WEB's “a man” is a translator supply — through the self-inflicted trouble of web:Ps.7.13-web:Ps.7.16, “His violence shall come down on the crown of his own head” (web:Ps.7.16), and closes on the psalmist's own vow, אוֹדֶ֣ה (web:Ps.7.17 = oshb:Ps.7.18, byte tier), “I will give thanks to Yahweh according to his righteousness, and will sing praise to the name of Yahweh Most High” (web:Ps.7.17). The presentative הִנֵּ֥ה opening web:Ps.7.14 (oshb:Ps.7.15), two verses into this strophe, is the psalm's unambiguous marker of the wicked man's third-person onset. The closing vow is grouped with the wicked man's downfall rather than set apart, since it functions as the psalm's response to that downfall rather than opening a new petition.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Setting the closing vow (web:Ps.7.17) apart as its own row was considered but rejected because a one-verse row would break the psalm's tiling into an unusually small unit without an independent seam signal separating it from web:Ps.7.16.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens with the conditional אִם לֹ֣א (web:Ps.7.12 = oshb:Ps.7.13, byte tier), shifting the subject from Yahweh to an unrepentant 'man' described in the third person

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 8's title (web:Ps.8.0 = oshb:Ps.8.1) marks it lamnatseach, on the gittith, le-David, and the nine verses form one hymn on human dignity framed by a returning refrain: the invocation “Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth” opens the psalm (web:Ps.8.1) and recurs to close it (web:Ps.8.9), bracketing the meditation on the heavens (web:Ps.8.3-web:Ps.8.4) and human dominion (web:Ps.8.5-web:Ps.8.8). The refrain's shared clause collates at byte tier against its own verse (web:Ps.8.1 = oshb:Ps.8.2) and at skeleton tier against the closing verse (web:Ps.8.9 = oshb:Ps.8.10): the two occurrences differ by a meteg (U+05BD), which the accent_stripped tier retains by design, so the pair matches at 1 of 4 collation tiers (skeleton) though the consonantal wording recurs; the closing verse omits the opening verse's second clause, “You have set your glory above the heavens” (web:Ps.8.1), rather than repeating it in full.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Dividing the psalm into a frame row and a body row at the refrain boundary was considered but rejected because the returning refrain argues for treating the hymn as one bracketed composition rather than cutting it at its own frame.

edited_rows.rationale: The mizmor's lamnatseach/le-David superscription, with its al-muth-labben tune name (web:Ps.9.0 = oshb:Ps.9.1), opens onto a self-referential cohortative vow — “I will give thanks to Yahweh with my whole heart” (web:Ps.9.1) — continuing through the parallel vow of praise in verse 2. The address stays second-person toward Yahweh as the ground of that vow follows: enemies who “stumble and perish in your presence” (web:Ps.9.3) because “you have maintained my just cause” (web:Ps.9.4). This second-person address to Yahweh persists past this strophe's own close, through web:Ps.9.5-web:Ps.9.6 (oshb:Ps.9.7); third-person description of Yahweh's reign begins 1 verse later, at web:Ps.9.7 (oshb:Ps.9.8).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A break isolating verse 1 alone as an opening line was rejected because the cohortative vow continues unbroken into verse 2 before the enemies-defeated ground clause begins.

edited_rows.device_notes: The rows here belong together under Psalm 9. Psalms 9 and 10 carry one irregular acrostic sequence running across both compositions, opening on a paired aleph at verses 1-2 (tier-1 surface letter data) before the letter pattern breaks — a typed cross-psalm relation; the pair stays two independent rows, not one merged row. The Greek Psalter numbers the pair as one composition (LXX 9 = MT 9-10 combined), a numbering-only crosswalk, not boundary evidence.

edited_rows.rationale: Continuing straight from the enemies’ defeat, the address turns to Yahweh’s universal acts of judgment: “You have rebuked the nations…You have destroyed the wicked” (web:Ps.9.5) gives way at verse 7 to third-person description — “Yahweh reigns forever” (web:Ps.9.7) — of his eternal throne, righteous judgment of “the world” (web:Ps.9.8), and refuge for “the oppressed” (web:Ps.9.9), closing on those who trust in Yahweh, “for you, Yahweh, have not forsaken those who seek you” (web:Ps.9.10). The strophe ends before the following imperative summons to communal praise.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the strophe at the second-to-third-person shift between verses 6 and 7 was rejected because both halves elaborate the one theme of Yahweh’s judgment of the nations and refuge for the oppressed without an accompanying imperative or vocative marker to justify a break.

edited_rows.rationale: An imperative onset — “Sing praises to Yahweh, who dwells in Zion” (web:Ps.9.11) — opens a call to communal praise grounded in Yahweh’s remembering “the cry of the afflicted” (web:Ps.9.12), then turns to the psalmist’s own petition, “Have mercy on me, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.13), continuing through the vow to “rejoice in your salvation in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (web:Ps.9.14). The strophe closes on the nations “sunk down in the pit that they made” (web:Ps.9.15) and the declaration “Yahweh has made himself known… The wicked is snared by the work of his own hands” — which the verse’s own Selah closes (web:Ps.9.16 = oshb:Ps.9.17), a tier-3 corroboration of the strophe’s end.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Isolating verse 16 alone as a Selah-marked coda was rejected because the verse's declaration “He has executed judgment.” (web:Ps.9.16) completes the nations' downfall reported in verse 15 rather than opening a new unit.

Don’t let man prevail” (web:Ps.9.19), continuing “Put them in fear, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.20). The psalm’s second Selah closes the verse and the composition (web:Ps.9.20 = oshb:Ps.9.21), a tier-3 corroboration matching the close that ended the previous strophe at Ps.9.16 (oshb:Ps.9.17), where the earlier Selah falls.

edited_rows.rationale: Untitled, Psalm 10 opens directly on a vocative lament question — “Why do you stand far off, Yahweh?” (web:Ps.10.1) — addressed to Yahweh in the second person, then turns in the third person to the portrait of “the wicked” that dominates the rest of the psalm: hunting “the weak” (web:Ps.10.2), boasting and condemning Yahweh (web:Ps.10.3), and having “no room in his thoughts for God” (web:Ps.10.4). The strophe closes before the extended description of the wicked’s methods that follows.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Limiting the opening unit to verse 1 alone was rejected because the third-person portrait of the wicked beginning at verse 2 continues without an intervening imperative or vocative through verse 4.

edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 10's rows converge on one parent grouping. Psalm 10 continues the irregular acrostic begun in Psalm 9 (typed cross-psalm relation; Psalm 10 keeps its own parent and is not merged with Psalm 9). Psalm 10 carries no superscription — 1 of 8 psalms in this span (Psalms 9-16) without a title. The second-person address to Yahweh that opens the psalm at web:Ps.10.1 recurs once more, embedded in the suffix of מִ֭שְׁפָּטֶיךָ (oshb:Ps.10.5, which carries an unrelated ketiv/qere pair earlier in the same verse), rendered “your laws” in the WEB (web:Ps.10.5), immediately past this row's own close, before the third-person wicked-catalog device proper begins at web:Ps.10.6.

edited_rows.rationale: Framed by two matching inner-speech formulas — “He says in his heart” opening its report of self-deceived confidence (web:Ps.10.6) and reopening its report of denial (web:Ps.10.11) — the device-bounded catalog of the wicked one's methods proper runs web:Ps.10.6-web:Ps.10.10: a cursing and deceitful mouth (web:Ps.10.7), ambush and murder of the innocent (web:Ps.10.8), lion-like predation on the helpless (web:Ps.10.9), and the helpless crushed under his strength (web:Ps.10.10). The strophe's opening verse (web:Ps.10.5 = oshb:Ps.10.5, which also carries an unrelated ketiv/qere pair) still carries second-person address to Yahweh through the embedded suffix in מִ֭שְׁפָּטֶיךָ (oshb:Ps.10.5), rendered “your laws” in the WEB, tying it to the vocative unit opened at web:Ps.10.1 rather than to the third-person catalog. The “He says in his heart” formula recurs a third time, cantillation-variant, at web:Ps.10.13, closing the catalog's own inclusio at web:Ps.10.6/web:Ps.10.11.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Breaking the strophe at verse 8 (villages/ambush) was rejected because no vocative, imperative, or inner-speech formula interrupts the predatory portrait between the two ‘says in his heart’ verses; the catalog reads as one continuous unit bounded by that repeated formula.

God, lift up your hand!” (web:Ps.10.12) — opens the psalm's closing plea, echoing the same imperative that opens Psalm 9's closing strophe (web:Ps.9.19; sweep: 6 verses book-wide open with this imperative). The wicked's rhetorical question, “God won't call me into account” (web:Ps.10.13), carries the same “says in his heart” inner-speech formula (אָמַ֥ר בְּ֝לִבּ֗וֹ, oshb:Ps.10.13) that frames the preceding strophe's catalog at web:Ps.10.6 and web:Ps.10.11 — its third, cantillation-variant occurrence — and is answered by the counter-claim “you do see trouble and grief” (web:Ps.10.14); the strophe closes on the imperative “Break the arm of the wicked” (web:Ps.10.15).

edited_rows.rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (web:Ps.11.0 = oshb:Ps.11.1) opens one 7-verse movement: refuge declared in the psalmist's own voice (“In Yahweh, I take refuge” web:Ps.11.1) against a quoted taunt to flee — the taunt's verb carries a ketiv/qere pair inline in the MT (נודו/נ֝֗וּדִי, oshb:Ps.11.1) — answered by a rhetorical question about the foundations (web:Ps.11.3), then Yahweh's heavenly examination of the righteous and the wicked (web:Ps.11.4-5), the wicked's judgment (web:Ps.11.6), and a closing confession of Yahweh's own righteousness (web:Ps.11.7). At 7 verses the psalm stays under the whole-psalm threshold, and no imperative or vocative shift interrupts its one sustained argument from refuge through vindication.

edited_rows.rationale: The lamnatseach/al-hashsheminit/mizmor/le-David superscription (web:Ps.12.0 = oshb:Ps.12.1) opens a cry over failing faithfulness (“Help, Yahweh” web:Ps.12.1) and flattering deceit (web:Ps.12.2-4), pivots at its center to a quoted divine oracle — “I will now arise,” says Yahweh (web:Ps.12.5) — and closes with confession of Yahweh's flawless words (web:Ps.12.6) and their promised protection (web:Ps.12.7) against the pervasive wicked (web:Ps.12.8). At 8 verses the psalm sits at the whole-psalm threshold; the oracle at its center corroborates rather than divides it, since no imperative or vocative brackets a seam on either side.

edited_rows.rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (web:Ps.14.0 = oshb:Ps.14.1) opens a diagnosis of universal corruption: “The fool has said in his heart” that “There is no God” (web:Ps.14.1), Yahweh's heavenly search from heaven (web:Ps.14.2) finding “no one who does good, no, not one” (web:Ps.14.3), and a rhetorical charge against the “workers of iniquity” who “don't call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4). The psalm turns at verse 5 to the righteous under Yahweh's refuge (web:Ps.14.5-6) and closes on a wish for Israel's restoration from Zion (web:Ps.14.7). At 7 verses it stays under the whole-psalm threshold, with no imperative or vocative shift marking an internal seam.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Breaking the psalm between the diagnosis (verses 1-4) and the refuge/restoration close (verses 5-7) was rejected because doing so would leave a 3-verse closing unit under the 4-verse strophe floor, with no imperative or vocative marking that seam.
observed_substrate_signals: the fool's inner speech opens the psalm in direct quotation (“There is no God” web:Ps.14.1), echoed by the finding “no one who does good, no, not one” (web:Ps.14.3); the shorter clause “no one who does good” (web:Ps.14.1, web:Ps.14.3) recurs at 2 of 7 verses within this psalm (verses 1 and 3)
the doublet’s shared opening clause is book-wide unique to two psalms (sweep: 2 verses, Ps.14.1 and Ps.53.1)
the divine name Yahweh (not a generic term for God) is used at verse 4’s “don’t call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4), part of Book I’s Yahweh-dominant texture
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 14's row answers to one parent composition. Psalm 14 opens with the same fool's-denial declaration that opens Psalm 53 (web:Ps.14.1; sweep: 2 verses book-wide share this opening, Ps.14.1 and Ps.53.1) and shares its “no one who does good” clause with Psalm 53 at 4 verses book-wide (Ps.14.1, Ps.14.3, Ps.53.1, Ps.53.3); the two stand as the book's doublet pair (typed relation, independent parents, kept as two separate rows here). The doublet's wording diverges at all 6 parallel verse pairs, with divine-name substitution accounting for 3 of them; one instance is Psalm 14's fourth verse, which names Yahweh as the object of its verb — “don't call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4) — where the parallel verse in Psalm 53 uses a generic term for God instead.

edited_rows.rationale: The mizmor's le-David superscription (web:Ps.15.0 = oshb:Ps.15.1) opens a question addressed to Yahweh — “who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?” (web:Ps.15.1) — answered by an unbroken catalog of the righteous person's qualities running verses 2-5: the MT carries 0 relative particles across web:Ps.15.2-web:Ps.15.5, instead alternating asyndetic participles — הוֹלֵ֣ךְ, 'walking' (oshb:Ps.15.2); נִבְזֶ֤ה and נִמְאָ֗ס, 'despised… rejected' (oshb:Ps.15.4) — with negated finite-verb clauses — לֹֽא רָגַ֨ל, 'has not slandered' (oshb:Ps.15.3); לֹא נָתַ֣ן and לֹ֥א לָ֫קָ֥ח, 'has not given… has not taken' (oshb:Ps.15.5) — bounded by the question at web:Ps.15.1 and the verdict clause “He who does these things shall never be shaken” (web:Ps.15.5). At 5 verses the psalm stays under the whole-psalm threshold as one question-and-answer unit.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the catalog of qualities in verses 2-5 into two shorter units was rejected because the asyndetic participial/negated-finite catalog runs continuously without any independent imperative or vocative marker to justify a break, and both halves would fall under the 4-verse strophe floor.
observed_substrate_signals: an opening question addressed to Yahweh (web:Ps.15.1) is answered by an asyndetic catalog spanning verses 2-5 that carries 0 relative particles, alternating participial and negated-finite clauses instead (sweep: 0 instances of the relative particle in oshb:Ps.15.2-oshb:Ps.15.5)
no imperative or vocative shift interrupts the catalog

edited_rows.rationale: Guidance language opens this strophe — “I will bless Yahweh, who has given me counsel” (web:Ps.16.7) — continuing through the confession “I have set Yahweh always before me” (web:Ps.16.8) and the resulting gladness (web:Ps.16.9). The strophe closes on resurrection confidence, “you will not leave my soul in Sheol” (web:Ps.16.10), and the psalm’s final vision of “the path of life” and “pleasures forever more” in Yahweh’s presence (web:Ps.16.11).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting this strophe at the shift from counsel (verses 7-9) to the Sheol confession (verses 10-11) was rejected because the closing pair alone (verses 10-11, 2 verses) would fall under the 4-verse strophe floor; a genuine addressee shift does mark that seam (web:Ps.16.7-web:Ps.16.8 refer to Yahweh in the third person, “I will bless Yahweh, who has given me counsel”; web:Ps.16.10-web:Ps.16.11 address Yahweh directly in the second person, “For you will not leave my soul in Sheol”), but the floor count independently controls the outcome.
observed_substrate_signals: counsel and confidence language runs verses 7-9 without an intervening imperative or vocative
the psalm’s closing confession names Sheol directly (“you will not leave my soul in Sheol,” web:Ps.16.10), continuing without a break into the path-of-life close (web:Ps.16.11)
no Selah falls within this strophe’s span-relevant set (Psalm 16 has no Selah-marked verse)

edited_rows.rationale: The title “A Prayer by David.” (web:Ps.17.0 = oshb:Ps.17.1) opens with תְּפִלָּ֗ה לְדָ֫וִ֥ד, tefillah le-David, a superscription genre label (tier-1 opener class) echoed within the same MT verse by תְפִלָּתִ֑י, 'my prayer,' in “Give ear to my prayer that doesn't go out of deceitful lips” (web:Ps.17.1). The vocative-imperative cluster “Hear, Yahweh, my righteous plea. Give ear...” (web:Ps.17.1) and the jussive petition “Let my sentence come out of your presence” (web:Ps.17.2) open a plea for a verdict that the psalmist grounds in sworn self-testimony through “My steps have held fast to your paths. My feet have not slipped” (web:Ps.17.5), so the appeal and its supporting testimony read as one continuous unit addressed to Yahweh, with the next vocative-imperative cluster resuming at web:Ps.17.6.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Isolating web:Ps.17.1-web:Ps.17.2 as its own strophe remains an open rival reading: the MT shows a genuine mood shift at the 17:2|17:3 seam — the imperative/yiqtol petition of web:Ps.17.1-web:Ps.17.2 gives way to a run of 3 2ms qatal declaratives opening web:Ps.17.3-web:Ps.17.5, 0 of those 3 verse-initial tokens carries a waw or subordinator — and no syntactic dependency ties the two halves together; this span is retained without a warrant that answers that shift.
observed_substrate_signals: title תְּפִלָּ֗ה לְדָ֫וִ֥ד (oshb:Ps.17.1) is a genre-label superscription, tier-1 opener class
the title's prayer-noun is echoed by תְפִלָּתִ֑י within the same MT verse (oshb:Ps.17.1)
imperative verbs cluster at the verse's open (“Hear... Give ear...”, web:Ps.17.1); the next such cluster sits at web:Ps.17.6
edited_rows.device_notes: This psalm's rows nest under one Psalm-17 parent.

edited_rows.rationale: A fresh petition cycle opens the strophe with a fronted pronoun and qatal verb, “I have called on you, for you will answer me” (web:Ps.17.6), echoing the psalm's opening plea (web:Ps.17.1); the vocative “God” and the imperatives “Turn your ear to me. Hear my speech” follow within the same verse. The imperatives continue through protective imagery, “Keep me as the apple of your eye. Hide me under the shadow of your wings” (web:Ps.17.8) — whose 1cs suffix already supplies the imperative's object — into the ablative complement “from the wicked who oppress me, my deadly enemies, who surround me” (web:Ps.17.9), which names the source of the danger rather than opening an independent third-person indictment; that indictment begins at web:Ps.17.10.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting web:Ps.17.6-web:Ps.17.7 from web:Ps.17.8-web:Ps.17.9 was considered but rejected because the imperatives that open both halves — “Hear my speech” (web:Ps.17.6) and “Keep me… Hide me” (web:Ps.17.8) — continue one uninterrupted petition, not because either half depends syntactically on an object clause carried by the other.
observed_substrate_signals: a fronted pronoun and qatal verb open web:Ps.17.6 (“I have called on you”); the vocative “God” (token 5 of 10) and the imperatives “Turn your ear” (token 6) and “Hear” (token 9) follow within the same verse, echoing the imperative cluster opening web:Ps.17.1

the imperative “Hide me… under the shadow of your wings” (web:Ps.17.8) already supplies its own object via the 1cs suffix; web:Ps.17.9 opens with an ablative complement (oshb:Ps.17.9) naming the source of danger, not an object clause, and carries 0 relative particles in its second colon
edited_rows.device_notes: No selah interrupts web:Ps.17.6-Ps.17.9.

edited_rows.rationale: The subject shifts from direct address of Yahweh to third-person description of the enemies — “They close up their callous hearts. With their mouth they speak proudly” (web:Ps.17.10) — continuing through the lion simile “He is like a lion that is greedy of his prey... lurking in secret places” (web:Ps.17.12); direct address of Yahweh resumes at web:Ps.17.13 (“Arise, Yahweh, confront him.”), which begins the following strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Grouping this third-person indictment with the imprecation that follows would obscure the address shift back to Yahweh that opens the next strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: third-person verbs (“They close up”, “they speak”, web:Ps.17.10; “surrounded”, web:Ps.17.11) replace the second-person address of the prior strophe across web:Ps.17.10-web:Ps.17.11; web:Ps.17.12's lion description is a verbless clause in the MT (its “is” is WEB-supplied), so it is not counted among these
the vocative 'Yahweh' + imperative 'Arise... confront him' reopen direct address at web:Ps.17.13
edited_rows.device_notes: No selah interrupts web:Ps.17.10-Ps.17.12.
